Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

edaphos 0.9.0 (development version — not yet released)

edaphos is a research package for digital soil mapping beyond regression-tree models, organised around ten methodological pillars: (1) causal inference — backdoor adjustment on pedogenetic DAGs, instrumental variables, Cinelli–Hazlett sensitivity, and LLM knowledge-graph extraction; (2) physics-informed ML — a parametric pedogenetic ODE and a differentiable Neural ODE; (3) 4D pedometry — stacked ConvLSTM with an Ensemble Kalman Filter; (4) foundation models — SimCLR / MoCo-v2 contrastive pre-training on raster patches; (5) autonomous active learning; (6) quantum ML — a ZZFeatureMap state-vector simulator and quantum kernel ridge regression; (7) Bayesian hierarchical spatial models (Gibbs / RcppArmadillo); (8) neural operators (DeepONet, Fourier Neural Operator); (9) diffusion models (DDPM) for soil-map patches; and (10) graph attention networks. A unified edaphos_posterior class lets seven of the ten pillars be scored with the same calibration diagnostics; Pillars 8, 9 and 10 have no coercion method and are absent from that comparison. The deep-learning pillars default to backend = "auto" — the trained torch model when a working libtorch is present, otherwise a pure-R reference path.

This is the first development version being prepared for submission; the API is not yet stable.

Development status

The package has never been released. Earlier NEWS.md carried 43+ version-numbered sections (0.8.0 → 4.1.0) written within a single development sprint; those were internal labels, not releases — the git tags run only to v1.6.0 and then jump to v3.10.0 / v4.0.0, and nothing named edaphos is on CRAN. Those sections are preserved in the git history; NEWS.md is reset here to a single honest development entry. Live, measured status (test counts, check result, install size) is generated into STATUS.md and cran-comments.md by the scripts in tools/status/, not written by hand.

Pillar 2 reworked around the equation’s closed-form solution

The depth-profile ODE dy/dz = -lambda0 * exp(-mu*z) * (y - y_inf) is separable and has an analytic solution. Using it instead of a numerical integrator exposed a mislabelling and a mis-parameterisation that had propagated into the shipped results, the active-learning gate and the manuscript.

  • y_inf is not the deep asymptote and is no longer reported as one. Since the rate decays with depth, the profile traverses only 1 - exp(-kappa) of the y0 -> y_inf gap, with kappa = lambda0/mu, and settles at y(Inf) = y_inf + (y0 - y_inf) exp(-kappa). Across the 1,105 shipped WoSIS profiles the median kappa is 1.6, so the median profile closes 80% of its gap and stops; on shallow profiles the two quantities routinely differ in sign. print() now labels y_inf as an ODE coordinate and reports y(Inf) and kappa alongside it.
  • The model is estimated in the identified, positive coordinates (y0, A, kappa, mu) with A = y(Inf), all exponentiated; lambda0 and y_inf are recovered unchanged for the public interface. Refitting 207 multi-horizon WoSIS profiles under both parameterisations: the old one returned a physically inadmissible fit for 116 of them (56%) — 113 with mu < 0, a decay rate growing exponentially with depth, and two with negative surface carbon — against none under the new one. Genuinely ascending profiles (argillic clay) are still fitted as such.
  • The posterior now identifies what matters. On the shipped pedon the 95% interval for the attainable deep value is [0.95, 4.48] g/kg, against [−20.5, 3.2] for the quantity previously reported as the asymptote: 6.7 times narrower and no longer reaching into impossible values. summary() gains kappa and y_asym rows, and the Bayesian priors are placed on the identified coordinates rather than on y_inf.
  • al_physics_gate_piml() no longer certifies negative carbon as plausible. Its envelope was built from y_inf; it is now the range the solution actually spans, floored at zero. See the section below for the measured effect on 300 real pedons.
  • Horizon-average observation operator. piml_profile_fit() and piml_profile_fit_bayesian() accept top/bottom horizon boundaries and compare each datum to the model’s depth-average over its horizon (8-node Gauss–Legendre on the closed form) rather than to a point evaluation at the mid-depth. Across 207 profiles this moves the fitted y0 by a median 0.28 g/kg and the deep value by 0.03 – the correction is concentrated in the thick, strongly curved surface horizons.
  • The L2 regulariser is centred on the data-driven start. It previously penalised the raw y_inf, so it scaled with the square of the property’s units and silently did part of the fitting: on the aqp::sp4 colusa pedon it pinned y_inf at 61.9% clay, which the README reported as the argillic-horizon asymptote. The same four horizons with the penalty removed give 533%. The number was imposed, not estimated.
  • piml_profile_fit() reports an extrapolation diagnostic. The new progress component is the fraction of the y0 -> y(Inf) journey the deepest horizon actually travelled; below 0.5 print() states that the deep value is an extrapolation rather than an estimate. It flags two of the ten aqp::sp4 pedons, and neither of those two beats a straight line. Two companion diagnostics, surface_ratio and in_scope, were added later.
  • A non-positive observed value is now an error rather than a silent fit, and the fitter uses several starting points instead of one.
  • Evaluating the closed form is ~281x faster than integrating with deSolve and agrees with it to 4e-5 g/kg; the equivalence is pinned in tests/testthat/test-piml-closed-form.R.
  • The Pillar-2 parameter table in inst/extdata/capstone_campaign_results.rds was regenerated from a real Laplace fit under the new parameterisation, and again after the pedon was replaced with a real WoSIS profile (below).

Pillar 2 refitted to real data, and its domain declared

A panel of five specialist pedometric reviewers read this pillar. Four of the five gave the same worst problem, and it was not the parameterisation: the pillar was calibrated on seven numbers typed into data-raw/capstone_campaign_run.R while 1,105 real multi-horizon WoSIS Cerrado profiles sat unused in tools/case_cerrado/, downloaded by this repository’s own scripts, which then kept only the shallowest horizon of each.

  • Real data. data-raw/piml_wosis_multihorizon.R keeps every horizon: 1,105 profiles, 5,853 horizons, median 150 cm and maximum 740 cm, shipped as inst/extdata/piml_wosis_cerrado.rds. The capstone pedon is now WoSIS profile 1115679 — nine horizons to 550 cm — selected by a criterion fixed before any fit was inspected.
  • A derivable alternative. piml_profile_fit_mechanistic() implements the advection-reaction limit of the standard soil-carbon depth balance, v dC/dz = I(z) - kC with root input I(z) = I0 exp(-z/z_r): constant rate, depth-varying target. Closed form, analytic layer averages, every parameter positive with a literature prior. It fits the shipped pedon markedly better (RMSE 0.44 vs 2.52), but across the profiles in the model’s domain the two are statistically indistinguishable once both are fitted with a correct likelihood — see the likelihood section below, which cost this entry its original claim.
  • A benchmark, reported whatever it says. data-raw/piml_depth_benchmark.R runs two pre-declared tasks over all 1,105 profiles against six competitors, including an equal-area spline and a pooled depth-as-covariate random forest. On mean absolute error the mechanism helps – 1.82 g/kg for the ODE against 2.06 for copying the nearest measured horizon and 2.67 for the random forest, winning the paired comparison against every baseline. On RMSE every method lands near 14 g/kg, because ten profiles carry 99% of the squared error; the gap between the two statistics is itself the finding. The equal-area spline does not extrapolate and abstains from the second task, which is reported rather than papered over. The restriction to the model’s domain was originally computed in a way that leaked the held-out horizon; see the method-defects section below.
  • The domain is now declared and enforced. lambda0 > 0 with a first-order relaxation makes the solution monotone, so an argillic bulge, an E horizon under an A or a buried A cannot be represented. 15.4% of the shipped profiles are not monotone even in their training horizons, and those that break monotonicity only at the horizon being predicted cannot be excluded in advance at all. piml_profile_fit() records in_scope, progress (how far the deepest horizon travelled toward y(Inf)) and surface_ratio (y0 reached 775 g/kg on one real profile), and print() says so.

The parameters were confronted with something outside the fit

Pillar 2 claimed its parameters were identified and interpretable. Identified it demonstrated; interpretable it asserted. data-raw/piml_external_anchors.R tests two directional predictions the mechanism makes and a curve-fitting device does not. They come out differently, and both are reported.

  • Hassink (1997) saturation: passes, weakly. If y(Inf) is a mineral-associated floor it must rise with clay + silt. Across 812 monotone profiles with a texture estimate within 5 km it does — slope +0.0067 per percentage point, p = 0.03, Spearman rho = 0.10 — and the attained value of the attenuating-rate form gives the same sign more strongly (p = 0.002). Texture explains 0.5% of the variance, though, and it is a SoilGrids prediction from a product trained partly on the same WoSIS archive. Reported as consistent with the mechanism and much weaker than a confirmation.
  • Jobbagy & Jackson (2000) beta: fails, and is withdrawn as an anchor. The implied beta is plausible in level (median 0.971, 5-95% 0.957-0.980) but moves with nothing outside the fit: tree cover R^2 = 0.00003, clay R^2 < 0.0001, precipitation R^2 = 0.0005. The one external variable it tracks is how deep the profile happened to be dug (R^2 = 0.024), a property of the survey. Meanwhile 63% of its variance is explained by our own fitted surface concentration. A statistic two-thirds determined by a parameter of the model it is meant to validate is not external evidence.

The constant-density assumption behind the beta calculation was measured rather than asserted: on the eight profiles carrying bulk density, computing the cumulative from mass rather than concentration moves the median beta by less than 0.0001.

Three method defects that invalidated published numbers

A full verification sweep of the specialist panel’s 266 findings – deduplicated to 190 unique defects and each re-checked against the current tree – surfaced three defects of method, not of implementation. Each one had produced a number that appears in the manuscript.

The benchmark’s skill column was scored against an oracle. edaphos_r2(truth, pred) divides by the variance of the test values about their own mean, which is computed from the very rows being scored. The manuscript’s Table 4 described that column as “measured against each fold’s training mean”, and its introduction states in as many words that scoring against the mean of the rows being scored is an oracle rather than a baseline. The roxygen of edaphos_r2() carried the same warning. The benchmark called it anyway. New edaphos_nse(observed, predicted, null_prediction) takes the null as a required argument and errors without it. Against the achievable null two methods score below zero, not three.

Spatially blocked folds had no buffer. The training set was the exact complement of the test block, with a measured minimum training-to-test distance of 15.2 km on the 1,095 benchmark profiles – well inside the range at which the fitted depth-function parameters are still correlated. (That range was given as 55-68 km from two identified parameters; re-running the variograms under the lognormal likelihood leaves ONE identified parameter, at 69 km.) New spatial_block_folds(coords, k, buffer_km, seed) discards training rows within the buffer, reports how many, and returns both the realised minimum distance and the one the unbuffered split would have allowed. At 68 km it costs 88 training rows across the five folds, 2.0% of the fold-wise training rows.

CORRECTED IN A LATER RELEASE. This entry originally read “Only one method moved: P10 GAT went from RMSE 0.617 to 0.679 … fifth place to last”, and gave the distance as 12.3 km. Both were wrong. 12.3 km belongs to the denser 3,077-profile causal extract, not to the benchmark. And the buffer comparison was made by hand, was never scripted, and does not reproduce – it also predated the correction of the Pillar-10 graph to great-circle distance, so it compared two different models. data-raw/buffer_effect.R now measures it: the buffer costs every method between 0.000 and 0.007 RMSE, the graph network the most, and the ranking is identical with and without it. The buffer is kept because it is the right protocol, not because it changes the answer.

The depth benchmark’s validity-domain stratifier read the held-out horizon. It judged a profile monotone from its complete record, including the deepest horizon that the extrapolation task holds out – so it excluded precisely the profiles whose held-out horizon jumps. Computed from training horizons only, as it must be, the subset grows from 875 to 935 profiles and the ODE’s RMSE goes from 1.51 to 14.74. The manuscript’s claim that declaring the validity domain moved the RMSE from 14.04 to 1.51 was an artefact of the leak; the largest jump in the held-out horizon is 17 g/kg among the profiles the leaking criterion admitted and 427 g/kg among those the honest one admits.

What replaced it is a better result. Ten profiles out of 935 – 1.1% – carry 99% of the squared error, and removing them takes the RMSE to 1.54. The median absolute error is 0.76 g/kg. The extreme case is a buried organic horizon, 430 g/kg at 125 cm with 3.0 g/kg immediately above it, and nothing available at fit time predicts it: the correlation between the size of the jump and the number of training horizons, the prediction depth, or the model’s own extrapolation diagnostic is below 0.03 in absolute value. A depth function fitted to the horizons above cannot know a buried horizon is coming, and no scope statement made from the same information can either.

The likelihood was wrong for a soil concentration

piml_profile_fit(), piml_profile_fit_bayesian() and piml_profile_fit_mechanistic() gain a family argument, and the default is now "lognormal" rather than Gaussian on g/kg.

A Gaussian likelihood on a concentration makes three errors. It places predictive mass below zero; it assumes additive error where laboratory error is multiplicative; and — the one that costs accuracy — it weights every horizon by the same absolute discrepancy, so a profile running from 29 g/kg at the surface to 2.3 g/kg at 5 m is fitted almost entirely by its topsoil while the deep horizons that carry the asymptote contribute almost nothing.

  • Both alternatives are parameterised so that the model’s prediction is the mean of the observation, and sigma is a coefficient of variation. Mean- preserving matters because the prediction is a horizon average, a mass- preserving quantity; a median-preserving lognormal would bias every layer down by exp(sigma^2/2).
  • On the shipped pedon the Gaussian fit misses the deepest horizon by 90% of its value; the lognormal caps its worst relative residual at 23%.
  • On leave-the-deepest-horizon-out prediction across all 1,105 WoSIS profiles the lognormal wins on 720 of them (paired Wilcoxon p = 2e-30), improving mean absolute error from 2.20 to 2.00 g/kg, and wins on RMSE too — even though RMSE is the criterion the Gaussian optimises by construction, because over-weighting the topsoil is what makes a profile extrapolate its deepest horizon badly. (These figures were first measured on a subset selected by the leaking stratifier described below and have been remeasured without it.)
  • predict() draws observation noise from the family the model was fitted with. Adding Gaussian noise to a positive fit would reintroduce the defect the argument exists to remove.

This changed a published conclusion. Under the Gaussian, the derived advection-reaction model appeared to beat the attenuating-rate ODE decisively on held-out prediction (p = 2e-6). Fitting both with a correctly specified likelihood removes the difference: MAE 1.76 against 1.82 g/kg, winning on 486 of 935 profiles against 449, p = 0.25. The Gaussian had been penalising the attenuating-rate form more, because over-weighting the topsoil hurts the model whose flexibility lies in the deep tail. The derived model is now recommended on the grounds that it can be derived, not on grounds of accuracy, where the honest answer is a tie.

Two related corrections to the native calibration table. Its predictive interval excluded observation noise while being scored against measured values, which a mean-function interval structurally cannot cover: restoring it takes the Pillar-2 PICP from 0.44 to 0.67, and the lognormal takes it to 0.78 while eliminating negative predictive draws entirely.

Inference and unit-consistency fixes

  • sigma is sampled, not plugged in. It was estimated once from the MAP residuals and held fixed through the whole MCMC — empirical Bayes that guarantees under-wide intervals. It now carries a half-t(3) prior; the predictive interval on the shipped pedon widens from 3.6 to 7.1 g/kg.

  • MCMC convergence is now reported. The sampler ran one chain and reported only an acceptance rate, so R-hat could not be computed even in principle. It now runs n_chains from dispersed starts and reports rank-normalised split-R-hat and bulk ESS (Vehtari et al. 2021), and print() says NOT CONVERGED when they fail. That immediately caught the old defaults: 5000/2000 gives max R-hat 1.015 and min ESS 361, against 1.004 and 1113 at 20000 iterations. The default is now the converging one.

  • The default prior is empirical Bayes and says so. Three of its hyperparameters are functions of the response. piml_prior_literature() provides a non-circular alternative built from published values, so the dependence can be measured rather than assumed harmless: on the shipped pedon it moves the attainable deep value from 2.22 [0.95, 4.48] to 2.45 [1.18, 4.56], so the circularity is not load-bearing here — but that is now a measurement rather than an assumption.

    EXTENDED IN A LATER RELEASE. That was one parameter of seven under one alternative prior, and reading “the circularity is not load-bearing” off it was too generous. data-raw/piml_prior_sensitivity.R now runs all seven under three priors, by MCMC on every arm and at a budget where all three converge. One parameter, mu, moves by more than half a posterior standard deviation (0.67); the rest move between 0.10 and 0.34. So the conclusion survives, narrowly, and it is concentrated on the depth-attenuation rate – the same parameter whose variogram fails to identify a range.

  • al_physics_gate_piml() no longer certifies negative carbon. Rebuilding its envelope from the attained value closed one route to a negative floor; the (safety_factor - 1) * span widening was the other. On 300 real WoSIS pedons the documented default gave a negative floor on 247 and accepted an SOC of -5 g/kg on 73. It now floors at zero for the parametric branch, which is by construction a fit to a positive property.

  • Pillar 3’s mass-balance loss divided by a z-scored mean. That mean is zero to machine precision, so the 1e-6 guard turned the outflow term into a 1e6 amplification: the physics residual arrived 2.6e7 times heavier than the data term, its sign flipped with the seed, and it destroyed the fit it was meant to regularise (fit loss 1.007 at physics_lambda = 1 against 0.085 at 0). temporal_convlstm_fit() now takes physics_scaling and forms the residual in the raw units the rate constants are written in. The same run now gives 0.072 against 0.085: the physics term helps for the first time. Without the scaling constants it errors rather than evaluating on the wrong scale.

Corrections to withdrawn pre-release notes

The withdrawn version-numbered notes contained claims that were never verified. They are corrected here rather than merely deleted:

  • “R CMD check: 0 errors / 0 notes” was never checked against a log; a real R CMD check --as-cran on the v3.10.0 tree produced 2 ERRORs, 1 WARNING and 6 NOTEs. All are fixed, and the current status is generated into cran-comments.md.
  • Test counts (“1 345 tests pass”, “1 308”, …) were quoted without their environment and did not always reconcile between sections. Current figures are measured into STATUS.md with platform and dependency context.
  • Pillar 1 × Pillar 4 (instrumental variables). Earlier notes and the README reported Sargan p = 0.343 / 0.283 / 0.424 and concluded that foundation-model embeddings are valid instruments. That run used placeholder normalisation (means = 0, sds = 1) over synthetic (noise) covariates. Re-run with a real MoCo-v2 encoder on real WoSIS Cerrado profiles, the embedding-PC instruments are strong (stage-1 F ≈ 1955) but fail the Sargan over-identification test (p ≈ 3×10⁻¹³): a learned representation does not manufacture a valid instrument. The README and the pilar1-pilar4-iv vignette now report this negative result, and tests/testthat/test-causal-real-bundle.R binds the figures to the shipped bundle so they cannot drift again.
  • Multi-backend LLM benchmark (Gemma 4 / GPT-4o-mini / Claude). The shipped bundle carried mode = "simulated" — a deterministic noise model, not measurements, with no API called. The vendor-attributed table was withdrawn. The causal-discovery “LLM-augmented” DAG, once six hand-typed edges, is now a real Gemma-4 extraction over the shipped Cerrado abstracts.

Nothing here changes what the code does; it changes what the project claims about what the code showed.
